text: That afternoon: Holmes remarks that so nice a bell-pull seems unnecessary, and excuses himself to examine the floor
why: ¶148 states Holmes finds so nice a bell-pull unnecessary and excuses himself to examine the floor; the visit is in the afternoon.

text: That afternoon: Holmes crawls over the floor with his lens, examining the cracks between the boards
why: ¶148 describes him crawling with his lens, examining the cracks between the boards.

text: That afternoon: Holmes examines the wood-work panelling in the same way
why: ¶148 says he then did the same with the wood-work panelling the chamber.

text: That afternoon: Holmes walks over to the bed and studies it and the wall
why: ¶148 says he walked to the bed and stared at it and ran his eye up and down the wall.

text: That afternoon: Holmes gives the bell-rope a brisk tug
why: ¶148 says he took the bell-rope and gave it a brisk tug.

text: What was the bell-rope put there for?
why: Holmes has openly queried the new and seemingly unnecessary bell-rope, so the question is natural and does not point at an answer.

text: What was the bell-rope put there for? — to ring for the housekeeper
why: Helen says in ¶143 that it goes to the housekeeper's room, so this is the obvious stated purpose.

text: What was the bell-rope put there for? — Julia did not ask for it, and the sisters always got what they wanted for themselves
why: ¶146-147: asked if her sister requested it, Helen answers no and says they always got what they wanted for themselves.
